text_en: I'm a visual person in general, so that's another thing — the description alone is a bit too little for me. I prefer to have the specimen in my hands. When I sometimes identify material someone collected, I always say: until you send me the dried specimen so I can make microscope preparations myself, I always have doubts, even if the photographic documentation is good. Another thing — and I warn you right away, because this may be a certain error in taking me as an expert — I'm someone who mainly uses a microscope for identifying mushrooms. That means that for a very large number of features... I very often work on dried material, so the features that exist are either only in photos, or sometimes I don't have a photo at all, and I notice, compared to my acquaintances who deal with mushrooms more as amateurs, that features they pay attention to on a fresh fruiting body — little details — I say: OK, I didn't pay attention to that at all, because for me these two species differ so much if I look at, say, the spore shape, that I never even looked for features that let you distinguish these fruiting bodies without looking into the microscope image. So in that respect it's certainly a bias and an error when comparing someone who works mainly with the microscope and someone who is a user who goes to the forest and will surely never put the mushroom under a microscope. That's what we call in the mycological community being 'well-acquainted' with some mushrooms, some group. Sometimes there are people who pay attention to such tiny, subtle differences that 'how do you know that?' — 'I don't know, it's just characteristic to me, you can see it right away.' And I say: 'and I don't see it, I have to glance under the microscope.' And conversely there are species I recognize without any error, and others say: 'how did you know?' — 'well, because it's minimally more brown, for example.' But these are very fleeting features.

context_en: INT: And how do you react to there being difficulty in identifying the species described in this original record? || P: Because as I understand, you're now looking for that match, trying to identify the species based on the description of these macroscopic features — mainly macroscopic — taking into account the numerous gaps in the data too, because 'stipe base: absent.' || P: Yes. Based on the description... Yes, a lot of data is missing. Besides, as I said at the very beginning, I have no idea what this original dataset looked like, if only because I don't know North American mushrooms very well. If there's some pool of species there, and in this set... I understand that species occurring only in North America weren't discarded and only the shared ones chosen, then there could be a whole group of species that don't come to mind but which in reality are common there and are, say, edible or poisonous. So that's the first difficulty. The second is the absence of certain features one looks at — how the stipe surface looks, or the hymenophore type. By default I understand it's gilled, because that's how the dataset was given at the start; and we also know the gills are orange, but it's also hard to say — important from a mycologist's point of view — for example the way the gills attach, right? Whether these gills have some edging or not? That's missing; it's a fairly massive mushroom, so I'm trying to think what else it could be, given it started as inedible or poisonous — maybe some Hypholoma, maybe some Hebeloma (poisonpie); it's hard to say. But absolutely crucial to me — and suspicious — is why solely lengthening the stipe suddenly makes the algorithm change the classification, all the more since we don't quite know how these mushrooms were photographed at the start, and secondly the way fruiting bodies grow sometimes deforms the fruiting body itself — for example ones growing from places with a lot of fallen wood, the stipe pushes through a thick layer to finally form the cap. Then if someone yanks it hard, they pull it out with a terribly long stipe, and it can be quite a distortion. Yes, these are rare cases, but they should be taken into account too, so this set of features, for me as someone who works with mushrooms — European ones at least — is a bit too little to unambiguously classify this fruiting body into any specific systematic group. || INT: Thank you very much indeed. || P: I'm a visual person in general, so that's another thing — the description alone is a bit too little for me. I prefer to have the specimen in my hands. When I sometimes identify material someone collected, I always say: until you send me the dried specimen so I can make microscope preparations myself, I always have doubts, even if the photographic documentation is good. Another thing — and I warn you right away, because this may be a certain error in taking me as an expert — I'm someone who mainly uses a microscope for identifying mushrooms. That means that for a very large number of features... I very often work on dried material, so the features that exist are either only in photos, or sometimes I don't have a photo at all, and I notice, compared to my acquaintances who deal with mushrooms more as amateurs, that features they pay attention to on a fresh fruiting body — little details — I say: OK, I didn't pay attention to that at all, because for me these two species differ so much if I look at, say, the spore shape, that I never even looked for features that let you distinguish these fruiting bodies without looking into the microscope image. So in that respect it's certainly a bias and an error when comparing someone who works mainly with the microscope and someone who is a user who goes to the forest and will surely never put the mushroom under a microscope. That's what we call in the mycological community being 'well-acquainted' with some mushrooms, some group. Sometimes there are people who pay attention to such tiny, subtle differences that 'how do you know that?' — 'I don't know, it's just characteristic to me, you can see it right away.' And I say: 'and I don't see it, I have to glance under the microscope.' And conversely there are species I recognize without any error, and others say: 'how did you know?' — 'well, because it's minimally more brown, for example.' But these are very fleeting features. || INT: I think there's nothing more here, and now we'll move to the next slide. It's an informational slide.
